prompt: Match each term with what it measures.
hint: Backwards from the incident, or forwards from it?

pairs.right: How far back the last recoverable moment may be
How long until the system is usable again
The longest a change waits on a quiet server before archiving

right_distractors: How many backups are kept in the repository

prompt: Why does the lesson say that "none and none" is not a requirement?
hint: What happens to a target nobody can meet?

choices.text: Because zero loss is forbidden by PostgreSQL
choices.why: Zero loss for a lost server is possible, with synchronous replication; it has a price.

choices.text: Because RPO and RTO are set by the backup tool
choices.why: They are business decisions; the tool decides what is achieved.

choices.text: It was said before anybody saw the price
choices.why: Right. A target nobody can meet gets ignored, which is the same as having none.

choices.text: Because only RTO matters for a database
choices.why: Both matter, and for different failures.

prompt: Why is an RPO stated as time ("five minutes of orders") rather than as bytes of log?
hint: Who has to understand it?

choices.text: Time is what the business weighs
choices.why: Right. Five minutes of orders is a number of sales; 300 MB of log is nothing to them.

choices.text: Because log size cannot be measured
choices.why: It can; lesson 4 measured it with LSNs.

choices.text: Because PostgreSQL archives on a timer, never by size
choices.why: Segments are finished when full, and archive_timeout adds a timer.

choices.text: Because time is always smaller than bytes
choices.why: They are different units and cannot be compared.

prompt: A team has a replica a second behind the primary and says their RPO is one second. For which failure is that wrong?
hint: What does a replica do with a mistaken DELETE?

choices.text: The primary's disk failing
choices.why: For that, the replica has everything up to a second ago.

choices.text: The primary's server losing power
choices.why: Again the replica has nearly everything.

choices.text: A network cut between users and the primary
choices.why: Data is not lost; the users cannot reach it, which is an RTO matter.

choices.text: A mistaken DELETE
choices.why: Right. The replica copies the DELETE within a second; for that failure the replica gives no recovery point at all.

prompt: Why does `rpo.sql` cut `last_archived_wal` to its first 24 characters?
hint: What does a backup archive besides segments?

choices.text: Because segment names longer than 24 characters are corrupt
choices.why: They are not corrupt; they are a different kind of file.

choices.text: A backup history file came last
choices.why: Right: just after a backup, the last file archived is a backup history file whose name has a suffix. pg_split_walfile_name refuses that name, which is how the first version of the query failed.

choices.text: To drop the timeline from the name
choices.why: The timeline is the first eight characters, and they are kept.

choices.text: To make the query faster
choices.why: Speed is not involved.

prompt: On a quiet server with no `archive_timeout`, `since_last_archive` reads 40 minutes and `not_yet_archived` a few kilobytes. What would a disk failure now cost?
hint: Those kilobytes are on this server only.

choices.text: Nothing, because a few kilobytes is negligible
choices.why: A few kilobytes can be several orders; their size says nothing about their value.

choices.text: The changes of the last 40 minutes
choices.why: Right. Everything written since the last archived segment exists only here.

choices.text: Exactly one segment of 16 MB
choices.why: The loss is what was written, a few kilobytes, spread over 40 minutes.

choices.text: Everything since the last full backup
choices.why: The archive covers everything up to 40 minutes ago.

prompt: With `archive_timeout = '60s'`, what RPO does a quiet server achieve for a lost disk?
hint: Lesson 4.

choices.text: It makes the loss zero
choices.why: A change can still wait up to the timeout.

choices.text: Nothing, because quiet servers never lose data
choices.why: A quiet server can hold an order for hours without archiving it.

choices.text: It doubles the retention
choices.why: Retention is a different setting.

choices.text: About a minute, plus the push
choices.why: Right: the loss is bounded to about a minute plus the time to push. A segment with any change in it is closed and archived within the minute.

prompt: Put the parts of a recovery's downtime in the order they happen.
hint: You cannot restore what nobody has noticed.
items: Decide to restore, and to what
Check the copy and reconnect the application
trap: Detection and the decision come first and are often the longest; copying and replay are what the drill measures; nobody works until the copy is checked and the application points at it.

prompt: A restore spends most of its time replaying a week of log. Which lever shortens that most directly?
hint: A restore starts from the newest backup of any kind.

choices.text: More frequent backups, such as a daily differential
choices.why: Right. A restore then replays one day of log at most, not seven.

choices.text: A faster network between repository and server
choices.why: That speeds the copy; the replay is limited by applying the log.

choices.text: A longer archive_timeout
choices.why: That changes the RPO on a quiet server, not the replay.

choices.text: Keeping more full backups
choices.why: More old backups do not shorten replay from the newest.

prompt: The business needs zero data loss if the primary server is destroyed. What is the only lever that delivers it?
hint: Every other one leaves a gap.

choices.text: archive_timeout of one second
choices.why: A second is small and still not zero, and it fills the archive with empty segments.

choices.text: A streaming receiver with --synchronous
choices.why: The server does not wait for it unless told to, so a commit can still be lost.

choices.text: Synchronous replication
choices.why: Right. Every commit waits for a second server; that is the price.

choices.text: Hourly full backups
choices.why: Backups bound the loss to an interval; they never make it zero.

prompt: Which of the RPO levers in the lesson protects against a mistaken DELETE?
hint: Which ones copy every change as fast as they can?

choices.text: A replica, because it is a second copy
choices.why: It copies the DELETE too, within a second.

choices.text: Synchronous replication
choices.why: It copies the DELETE even more faithfully.

choices.text: A streaming receiver
choices.why: It receives the DELETE like everything else, which is fine: replay can stop before it, but the receiver alone does nothing.

choices.text: None of them: point-in-time recovery does
choices.why: Right. A mistake needs a copy you can stop before the mistake, and that is PITR from base backups and the archive.

prompt: In real incidents, which part of the downtime is often longer than the restore itself?
hint: The part before the first command.

choices.text: Copying the files back
choices.why: The drill measures that, and it is usually the shorter part.

choices.text: Replaying the log
choices.why: Long on a busy database, and measurable; the human part is the one that surprises.

choices.text: Noticing, deciding and finding the right person
choices.why: Right. Alerting, a runbook and rehearsal are the levers for those minutes.

choices.text: Compressing the backup
choices.why: Compression happens at backup time, not during the incident.

prompt: Why does the agreement have a column for the person who agreed to each number?
hint: Who decides on the day?

choices.text: They choose on the day
choices.why: Right: they decide between a quick restore and a careful repair. Somebody has to accept the loss, knowing the price of doing better.

choices.text: For the audit trail only
choices.why: The audit trail is useful; the column exists because that person decides during the incident.

choices.text: Because a team cannot sign anything
choices.why: Teams can agree; what matters is one person with the authority to accept the loss.

choices.text: So the DBA is not blamed
choices.why: Blame is not the point; authority is.

prompt: Why does the agreement record when each number was last measured?
hint: What happens to an RTO as the data grows?

choices.text: Because the law requires a date on every document
choices.why: The date is there for the engineering reason.

choices.text: Because the RTO grows with the data
choices.why: Right. The date says how much to trust the figure.

choices.text: Because the RPO changes every night
choices.why: The RPO is set by the setup; the RTO decays with growth.

choices.text: To know when to delete old backups
choices.why: Retention has its own setting.

prompt: Match each target with the cheapest setup in the lesson that meets it.
hint: The cost curve.

pairs.left: RPO of zero for a lost server

right_distractors: A weekly full backup with no archive

prompt: Forty seconds and three orders after the backup, how many kB of log existed only on the server?
hint: not_yet_archived.

prompt: The drill replayed about 2411 MB of log in 55.3 seconds. Roughly how many MB per second is that?
hint: Divide, and round.

prompt: A database writes 20 GB of log a day and takes only a weekly full backup. At 44 MB/s of replay, about how many minutes does replaying six days of log take? (1 GB = 1024 MB.)
hint: 6 × 20 × 1024 MB, divided by 44, then by 60.

prompt: Why should the replay rate be measured on the hardware that will do the restore?
hint: Who replays the log on the day?

choices.text: Because the live server cannot replay its own log
choices.why: It does so after every crash; the point is which machine restores.

choices.text: Because the archive is only readable from the restore server
choices.why: Any configured server can read it.

choices.text: The machine sets the replay rate
choices.why: Right: the rate depends on the machine that applies the log. A smaller restore server replays more slowly, and the promise is about that server.

choices.text: Because replay is faster on a quiet day
choices.why: The day matters too, but that is the other caution.

prompt: The agreed RTO for the orders database is one hour. The last drill took 40 minutes from restore to proof, and it was run on a quiet Sunday. What is the honest conclusion?
hint: What does the drill leave out, and on what day was it measured?

choices.text: Not yet shown: measure a busy day, and add the human minutes
choices.why: Right. Forty minutes of machine time on a quiet day says little about an hour on the worst one.

choices.text: The promise is met with twenty minutes to spare
choices.why: The drill leaves out noticing, deciding and reconnecting, and a busy day replays more log.

choices.text: The promise is broken, because 40 is close to 60
choices.why: Close is not broken; what is missing is the evidence for the worst day.

choices.text: The RTO should be raised to two hours just in case
choices.why: Changing the promise is legitimate, but only after measuring what the setup really does.
